title: I spent way too long cataloging Al game dev tools and ended up with 100+. The space is moving insanely fast
author: RepresentativeUse115
selftext:
I couldn't find a single up-to-date list of Al tools for game dev, so I made one. It's now over 100 tools in 20 categories.

The parts that surprised me most: 3D model generation is actually usable now (Hunyuan3D 2.1, TRELLIS.2), there are MCP servers that let an Al drive Blender, Godot, Unity and Unreal directly, and there's a whole Playtesting & QA category now. Pixel art (PixelLab, Retro Diffusion), music (ACE-Step) and NPC brains (Convai, Player2, NVIDIA ACE) all have their own sections too.

It's free and CCO: [github.com/aigamedevs/awesome-ai-tools-for-game-dev](http://github.com/aigamedevs/awesome-ai-tools-for-game-dev)

Honest question for people shipping stuff: which of these actually made it into your pipeline, and which ones turned out to be hype?

comments.author: FazedEclipse2
comments.body:
Plenty of good quality GAMES with poor pixel art part of the charm. Single minded must be the best graphics is what kills most AI projects.

Fact is for the average game maker that's the ceiling.

AI generation of pixel animation etc is awful and takes a lot longer, costs money and literally looks like AI slop.

comments.author: Arya_the_Gamer
comments.body:
Likely just injecting stuff in the blender by python scripts.

Most current frontier models can manually access stuff without the need of mcp.

Deepseek also is able to manage my godot game project without the need of mcp and uses the headless cli to run all the tests.

replies.author: New_Patience_8107
replies.body: I was having some issues via Godot and blender headless CLI. Now using the mcp but I also did some fine-tuning/debugging along the way. Could be it would've been fine without the mcp I'll keep it for the moment but agree don't think it's vital.

comments.author: scarecr0w12
comments.body:
MCP doesn't inherently give Blender different OS permissions. It gives the client a standard way to discover and call the tools a server exposes. What those calls can access depends on the server implementation, the account it runs under and any sandbox or approval checks around it. An MCP tool that accepts arbitrary Python can be just as broad as terminal access.

  
For your headless-versus-MCP comparison, the useful distinction is whether the latter is talking to the Blender session you already have open. A background process loading a saved .blend won't include unsaved edits in that open session. Check the file path, saved state and active scene before comparing the output; then try the same small operation on a copy through both routes. That helps separate a state/context problem from an interface problem.

  
If the terminal workflow already gives you repeatable results, there's no requirement to add MCP. A bridge earns its place when it provides something you need, such as access to the live scene or clearer structured results. The protocol itself isn't a sandbox: [https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18#security-and-trust-safety](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18#security-and-trust-safety)
